name: South Korea
summary_text: South Korea is broadly workable — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. But the country has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (a gap not shared by EU peers), no same-sex marriage, and a conservative society where 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers. Institutional friction is documented: the national human rights body flags a "transgender blind spot" in hospital wards (the Health Ministry can't answer how to accommodate trans patients); school bathrooms are a documented friction point for trans teens; and among trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military, 12% experienced sexual harassment or violence (this affects Korean conscripts, not foreign visitors). No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Legal gender recognition runs through the courts (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it). Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

sources.title: Police advice to LGBTQ+ individual to avoid public restrooms ruled as rights violation - The Korea Times
sources.claim_summary: Korea Times (July 2024): a court ruled that police advising an LGBTQ+ individual (undergoing gender correction) to avoid using public restrooms constituted an infringement of personal rights, awarding symbolic damages of 300,000 won - recognition that such remarks ignore the reality faced by LGBTQ people.

sources.title: Court rules against mandating transgender surgery to change legal sex status | Yonhap News Agency
sources.claim_summary: Yonhap (May 2024): a court ruled against mandating transgender surgery to change legal sex status - a significant ruling on the requirements for legal gender recognition in South Korea.

The Hankyoreh (March 2024): for trans teens in South Korea, even using school bathrooms involves safety questions - the youth support centre Dding Dong presented research on school practices that exclude trans students; first-person accounts of avoiding restrooms out of fear.

sources.title: Transgender blind spot in hospitalization: NHRCK - The Korea Herald
sources.claim_summary: Korea Herald (Nov 2023): the NHRCK (national human rights commission) flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalization' - the Health Ministry rejected a request to devise hospitalisation guidelines for trans patients; separate men's/women's rooms leave trans and nonbinary patients in a blind spot; hospitals were merely 'recommended' to place trans patients in single rooms.

sources.title: South Korea | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised in the military (Article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023) but legal for civilians; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (repeated proposals stalled); legal gender change requires medical intervention; the November 2022 Supreme Court ruling affirmed that having minor children is not grounds to refuse gender-marker change; intersex people largely unprotected.

sources.title: Being trans in Korea: key milestones and stigmatization across life stages in a nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults - PMC
sources.claim_summary: Peer-reviewed study (Epidemiology and Health, June 2025): 'Being trans in Korea' - nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults documenting key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages.

sources.title: World Report 2025: South Korea | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: HRW World Report 2025 South Korea chapter: overall positive human rights record amid political turmoil (martial law, impeachment); includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section.

misterb&b gay travel guide to South Korea safety (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods but requiring contextual understanding - military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry covers the South Korean Supreme Court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

sources.title: South Korea: Supreme Court Affirms LGBT Rights | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: HRW (Aug 2017): 'South Korea: Supreme Court Affirms LGBT Rights' - the National Health Insurance Service was ordered to pay benefits to a same-sex partner, affirming equal treatment; a significant judicial step amid the military's ongoing anti-gay witch-hunts.
